operationalization: Within well-sampled fossil lineages and formations, quantify morphometric intermediacy, stratigraphic spacing, and taxonomic rank. Test whether intermediates are uncommon and whether close forms from successive stages are routinely assigned separate species.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences, accepted taxonomy, formations, and geological ages

obstacles: Intermediate status depends on phylogeny and chosen characters.
Sampling and taxonomic practice vary strongly among clades and periods.
rationale: Occurrence and taxonomy data permit broad tests, but do not directly encode morphological intermediacy or historical naming practice. Focused clades can be resolved more convincingly than the full generalization.

operationalization: For genera and families, compare first appearances through successive database releases and model range extensions against sampling intensity. The claim is supported if improved sampling systematically pushes inferred origins earlier and reveals pre-radiation occurrences.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: dated fossil occurrences and taxonomic first appearances

obstacles: Absence below a boundary is intrinsically hard to distinguish from non-preservation.
Database revision history is not a controlled sampling experiment.
rationale: Large public fossil datasets directly support first-appearance and sampling analyses. They can establish pervasive range extension but cannot prove that every abrupt appearance is an artefact.

operationalization: Identify independently evolved ecological innovations, estimate waiting time to acquisition, subsequent diversification rates, disparity, and geographic spread, and compare these with sister groups lacking the innovation. Support requires consistently elevated post-innovation radiation and dispersal after a longer acquisition interval.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: synthetic phylogenies for comparing diversification around ecological innovations

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil timing, diversity, and geographic spread

obstacles: A 'peculiar way of life' and 'comparatively short' require subjective thresholds.
Innovation, diversification, and dispersal are confounded with environment and preservation.
rationale: Comparative phylogenetic and fossil analyses can test restricted examples such as flight. Available data and causal identification are too uneven for the broad mechanism as stated.

operationalization: Estimate the age and diversity of pre-Silurian life from radiometrically dated fossils, biomarkers, and molecular-clock analyses. Compare the duration before the Silurian and evidence of abundance with the Silurian-to-present interval and a minimal-life alternative.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: dated Precambrian and early Paleozoic fossil occurrences

obstacles: Early molecular clocks have broad calibration uncertainty.
Soft-bodied Precambrian life has a highly incomplete record.
'Swarmed' lacks a precise abundance threshold.
rationale: Public fossil and geochronological records strongly test the existence and duration of pre-Silurian life. They only partially resolve global abundance and Darwin's specific claim that the earlier interval was at least as long.

operationalization: Reconstruct Silurian-to-present continental crust, ocean basins, and paleoshorelines from plate models and geological constraints. Quantify overlap between ancient and present continental and oceanic areas; extensive changes would refute rough positional continuity.

candidate_datasets.name: GPlates
candidate_datasets.role: open plate-tectonic reconstruction software and published reconstruction data

obstacles: Most Silurian oceanic crust has been subducted.
The word 'roughly' permits multiple overlap thresholds.
rationale: Modern plate reconstructions make the spatial proposition explicit and strongly discriminating. Deep-time ocean-basin uncertainty remains, but existing data can clearly confirm or refute the broad stated inference.

operationalization: Estimate taxon first-appearance rates and clustering through time separately for terrestrial and aquatic records after standardizing sampling. Compare gradual asynchronous origination against simultaneous pulses at available temporal resolution.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: global fossil occurrences, environments, and first appearances

obstacles: Stage-level dating can make gradual appearances look simultaneous.
Preservation differs sharply between land and water.
rationale: The variables and alternatives map directly to standard paleobiological analyses. Global coverage is imperfect, but sufficient data exist to evaluate whether clustered pulses or slow succession better describe major intervals.

operationalization: Estimate lineage-specific morphological or molecular evolutionary rates and net character change across genera and classes. Test whether among-group rate variance exceeds measurement and sampling error and whether accumulated change differs among groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: public morphological character matrices across living and fossil taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: temporal occurrence framework for fossil groups

obstacles: Comparable characters are scarce across classes.
Taxonomic duration and preservation can inflate rate differences.
rationale: Heterogeneous evolutionary rates are directly measurable with established comparative methods and public matrices. Full cross-life comparability is limited, but the general claim is readily exposed to refutation.

operationalization: Compare standardized origination, extinction, turnover, and morphological rates for matched terrestrial and marine clades and time bins. Support requires consistently higher rates on land after controlling for preservation, taxonomy, and clade composition.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences classified by environment and age

obstacles: Terrestrial preservation and sampling are much poorer than marine preservation.
'Change' can mean turnover or morphological evolution.
rationale: The database supports direct environmental comparisons, but preservation creates a severe, directionally relevant confound. Restricted matched analyses are feasible; a global verdict is less secure.

operationalization: Search dated occurrence records for species with a substantial global absence followed by later occurrences, then audit taxonomy and dating. A validated reappearance of the identical biological species would refute the claim; no such cases supports it only within detection limits.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: species occurrence ranges and apparent temporal gaps

obstacles: Lazarus taxa usually reflect sampling gaps rather than true global extinction.
Morphospecies identity may not equal biological-species identity.
rationale: The universal prediction is clear and searchable in a large public record. Confirming non-reappearance is asymmetric and taxonomic identity is imperfect, but counterexamples can decisively refute it.

operationalization: For genera and families, identify gaps between dated occurrences and estimate sampling-adjusted probabilities of true absence. Confirm continuity when gap lengths match expected non-detection; validated extinction followed by renewed membership would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: dated occurrences and taxonomic membership of genera and families

obstacles: Higher-taxon boundaries are revised over time.
Poor sampling can create false disappearance and reappearance.
rationale: Continuity of higher taxa is directly testable with occurrence ranges and standard gap analyses. The fossil record cannot prove uninterrupted presence everywhere, but broad violations or support are resolvable.

operationalization: Construct sampling-standardized diversity trajectories for genera and families from first to last appearance. Estimate the fraction showing unimodal gradual rise-and-fall curves versus abrupt, flat, or multimodal histories.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: time-binned occurrences for taxonomic diversity trajectories

obstacles: Taxonomic practice affects species and genus counts.
Coarse bins can conceal abrupt changes.
rationale: This is a direct quantitative prediction about diversity trajectories, with abundant public occurrence data and standard methods. Sampling correction is necessary but does not prevent discrimination among trajectory shapes.

operationalization: Measure the temporal and geographic sequence of last occurrences for species and higher taxa, and quantify clustering at extinction horizons. Compare range contraction and staggered losses with globally synchronous abrupt disappearance.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: spatiotemporal fossil last occurrences and extinction-event records

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect makes abrupt extinction appear gradual.
Dating precision differs among regions.
rationale: Global fossil occurrences directly address extinction tempo and spatial sequence. Known sampling effects complicate direction, but event-specific models can distinguish many gradual and catastrophic patterns.

operationalization: For many clades, compare the duration and slope of diversity accumulation after origin with decline before extinction, correcting for sampling. Test whether extinction phases are generally longer and more gradual than origination phases.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: time-binned taxonomic diversity from origination to extinction

obstacles: Boundary choice and time-bin width affect apparent asymmetry.
Mass extinctions may dominate terminal slopes.
rationale: The predicted temporal asymmetry is explicit and estimable across many fossil clades. Data biases remain, but existing records and sensitivity analyses can resolve the general tendency.

operationalization: Estimate occupancy or abundance trajectories before last appearance in fossil species and before documented modern extinctions. Test whether declining rarity occurs more often than stable or increasing abundance immediately before extinction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence frequency and geographic occupancy before fossil last appearances

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: documented population trends and extinction status for modern species

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect can manufacture apparent pre-extinction rarity.
Occurrence counts are imperfect abundance proxies.
rationale: Both fossil occupancy and modern population trends are available at useful scale. Biases weaken causal interpretation but still allow a strong test of the stated empirical regularity.

operationalization: Estimate sampling-standardized global diversity, origination, and extinction rates across later geological intervals. Test whether long-run net diversification is near zero and whether origination covaries with losses, while separating balance from causation.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: global fossil diversity, origination, and extinction estimates

obstacles: Global species richness is incompletely sampled.
Rate balance does not show that new forms caused extinctions.
rationale: Existing data can test approximate numerical balance over selected periods. They have much less power to establish Darwin's causal interpretation or a global species-level ceiling.

operationalization: Reconstruct ancestor-descendant or close-relative sets and compare extinction risk following descendant origination as a function of ecological and phylogenetic similarity. Support requires elevated parent and congener extinction beyond environmental and background-rate controls.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil origination, extinction, and co-occurrence patterns

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic proximity among candidate competitors

obstacles: Direct parent-descendant relationships are rarely identifiable.
Shared environmental responses mimic competitive replacement.
Superiority is not directly observed.
rationale: Turnover among close relatives can be analyzed, but the decisive causal variables are rarely present. Existing data resolve proxies and selected systems, not the general mechanism.

operationalization: Compare dated marine assemblage turnover horizons among regions and climates using shared taxa and compositional change. Estimate global synchronicity relative to dating uncertainty and test whether fossil-based correlations outperform geography or climate alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: global dated marine fossil assemblages and taxonomic turnover

obstacles: 'Almost simultaneously' is scale-dependent.
Biochronological dating can be circular when fossils also define ages.
rationale: Marine biostratigraphy and global occurrence data directly target the proposition. Independent radiometric constraints can limit circularity, leaving a highly feasible and discriminating analysis.

operationalization: Within clades having morphological matrices, calculate distance from each fossil to extant relatives and regress it on fossil age while controlling for phylogeny and missing characters. A generally positive age-distance relation supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological character matrices containing fossil and living taxa

obstacles: Morphological matrices are curated for selected clades rather than all life.
Distance depends on character selection and extant survivor bias.
rationale: The relationship is measurable for many well-sampled clades, but no harmonized dataset spans the stated scope. Phylogenetic structure also makes a simple age-distance trend only moderately discriminating.

operationalization: Add fossil taxa to morphological phylogenetic matrices and measure whether disparity gaps and branch lengths among extant higher groups shrink. Refutation would be widespread fossils falling outside existing-group relationships or failing to reduce the specified gaps.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: published morphological matrices for integrating extinct and living taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: reference synthesis of taxonomic and phylogenetic relationships

obstacles: 'Fill gaps' lacks a unique quantitative definition.
Higher-group classification is partly constructed from the same characters being tested.
rationale: Selected clades permit explicit disparity and phylogenetic tests. The universal and classification-dependent wording prevents full resolution with a single non-circular analysis.

operationalization: For pairs of related higher groups, compare morphological distance between older fossil members and between extant members using homologous characters. Support requires smaller between-group distance in older strata specifically for groups with substantial later modification.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: fossil and extant morphological character matrices

obstacles: Suitable shared-character matrices exist for limited clades.
Early members can be mosaics without being mutually closer overall.
rationale: The prediction has measurable comparative consequences in clade-specific matrices. Dataset coverage and alternative distance definitions limit any assessment across all higher groups.

operationalization: Compute taxonomic or trait-composition similarity among fossil assemblages as a function of temporal separation, geography, and environment. Test for distance decay through time and whether each interval is compositionally intermediate between adjacent intervals.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: dated fossil assemblages for temporal similarity analysis

obstacles: Facies and geography can dominate temporal similarity.
Unequal sampling affects pairwise resemblance.
rationale: This maps directly to standard beta-diversity and temporal autocorrelation analyses. Broad public coverage and explicit controls make the general pattern resolvable despite uneven sampling.

operationalization: Use reconstructed traits, niches, and food webs to simulate competition between matched Eocene and extant assemblages under the same climate, or test temporal replacement where older and newer lineages overlapped. Consistent estimated competitive dominance by recent forms would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Eocene and recent occurrence and assemblage composition data

obstacles: Direct competition between extinct and living communities cannot be observed.
Most competitive traits and interactions do not fossilize.
Simulation results depend strongly on assumed mechanisms.
rationale: The counterfactual can only be approached through proxies or models built from incomplete traits. Existing data can examine overlap and replacement in selected lineages but cannot resolve certain extermination of whole faunas.

operationalization: For regions with late Tertiary fossils, compare fossil taxa's phylogenetic and morphological proximity to living regional taxa versus living taxa elsewhere. Support requires a significant same-region affinity after controlling for environment and spatial sampling.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: regional late Tertiary fossil occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global present-day species occurrences

obstacles: Continental boundaries and ranges shifted through time.
Extinction and dispersal can erase local descendants.
rationale: Fossil and modern occurrence data permit explicit same-region versus elsewhere comparisons. Phylogenetic harmonization is substantial but feasible for the highlighted vertebrate and molluscan groups.

operationalization: Model global assemblage taxonomic and phylogenetic similarity from climate and physical environment, then compare environmentally matched regions on different continents. The absolute wording is refuted if conditions explain most biotic similarity and supported if strong regional residuals remain.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global terrestrial species occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: global marine species occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: global climatic predictors

obstacles: Occurrence sampling is geographically biased.
Historical accessibility covaries with present environment.
rationale: Global occurrence and environmental datasets directly enable the stated comparison at large scale. Causal partitioning of history and environment is imperfect, but the strong claim is readily testable.

operationalization: Relate taxonomic and phylogenetic turnover across paired sites to barrier type, permeability, and age while controlling geographic distance and environment. Support requires larger differences across older or less permeable barriers.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global species distributions across terrestrial barriers

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: marine distributions across isthmuses and ocean barriers

obstacles: Barrier age and historical permeability can be uncertain.
Sampling effort changes abruptly at political borders.
rationale: This is a standard biogeographic hypothesis with extensive open occurrence data and clear comparative predictions. Multiple barrier replicates provide substantial discriminating power.

operationalization: Compare phylogenetic affinity of species occupying different habitats within a continent or sea against ecologically matched species on other continents or seas. Support requires geography to predict relatedness and replacement better than habitat similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global terrestrial and freshwater species occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: global marine occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic relationships for occurrence taxa

obstacles: Synthetic phylogenies have uneven resolution.
Habitat labels require harmonization.
rationale: The geography-versus-environment contrast is explicit and supported by global distributions and phylogenies. Coverage is broad enough for decisive tests across many clades.

operationalization: Test whether regional living and fossil assemblages share phylogenetic ancestry beyond environmental matching, then partition trait and lineage turnover among inherited regional history, selection-associated environment, and direct plastic responses. Support requires strong geographic phylogenetic continuity not explained by physical conditions.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: living regional distributions

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil regional distributions

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic affinity

obstacles: Inheritance, selection, and direct environmental effects are not cleanly separable observationally.
Fossil and living taxonomies are unevenly linked.
rationale: Regional phylogenetic continuity is testable with existing data. The asserted causal apportionment between natural selection and direct physical effects remains confounded and only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Compare phenotypic and genomic change after isolated colonization by intact multi-species assemblages versus single or compositionally disrupted colonists, controlling time and environment. Support requires little change in intact-group colonizations and more change when biotic relations shift.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public genomic, trait, and colonization datasets from individual natural experiments

obstacles: Intact community colonizations are rare and poorly replicated.
Migration changes abiotic conditions as well as species interactions.
'Little modified' lacks a universal scale.
rationale: The mechanism has measurable consequences, but relevant natural experiments are scattered and rarely isolate the proposed cause. Existing data can test case studies, not the broad counterfactual.

operationalization: Calculate geographic occupancy and regional endemism for families, subfamilies, genera, and infrageneric groups, then relate genus range to within-genus phylogenetic cohesion. Support requires many lower higher-taxa to be single-region and cohesive genera to be especially local.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global occurrence ranges across taxonomic ranks

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic hierarchy and phylogenetic cohesion

obstacles: Regions and 'natural genera' require explicit definitions.
GBIF coverage is uneven among taxa and countries.
rationale: Global taxonomic occurrence data permit direct rank-specific range calculations. The secondary claim about naturalness needs interpretation but is still testable using phylogenetic cohesion.

operationalization: For species with dense genomic and occurrence sampling, infer ancestral geographic origin and expansion history and test monophyly of populations against independent polycentric origins. Repeated well-supported single origins would support the generalization.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: public sequence data for population and species phylogeography

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: current occurrence ranges

obstacles: Species boundaries and geographic origins are often uncertain.
Extinction erases source populations.
A single-origin model can be difficult to distinguish from gene flow after multiple origins.
rationale: Modern phylogeography can strongly test selected species. Data are not adequate across all species, and deep origins are often non-identifiable from present descendants alone.

operationalization: Reconstruct paleogeography over the age range of extant species and test for continuous or nearly continuous emergent land corridors connecting modern continents to oceanic islands. Any securely dated continuous corridor would refute the relevant regional claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GPlates
candidate_datasets.role: plate and paleogeographic reconstructions

obstacles: The 'period of existing species' varies greatly among taxa.
Short-lived or submerged land connections may leave sparse evidence.
rationale: Plate, bathymetric, and geological data make continuous land connections a clear historical proposition. Uncertainty is region-specific, but major recent bridges can be confirmed or excluded with existing evidence.

operationalization: Compile published seawater flotation-duration and post-immersion germination experiments for a representative flora, combine survival time with current velocities, and estimate the fraction capable of 900-mile dispersal. Confidence intervals excluding 10 percent would refute Darwin's numerical estimate.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public supplements from seed buoyancy and saltwater-germination studies

obstacles: No known unified dataset samples a representative whole flora.
Ocean travel time depends strongly on route and seed state.
Published experiments may overrepresent dispersal-prone taxa.
rationale: The numerical claim is highly operational and discriminating, but needed species-level experimental data are fragmented. Existing studies can estimate the proportion for selected floras, not robustly for a generic flora.

operationalization: Estimate successful natural colonization rates across ocean distances using island floras, dated phylogeographies, currents, bird movements, and organismal dispersal traits. Test for a steep decline after hundreds of miles and near-zero exchange between distant continents.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: island and continental distributions

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: animal movement tracks relevant to transport vectors

obstacles: Observed disjunctions rarely identify the transport mechanism.
Rare long-distance events are hard to estimate from present ranges.
Human introductions contaminate modern distributions.
rationale: Distance decay and colonization histories are testable in many island systems. Attribution to Darwin's listed vectors and a universal distance cutoff remain only partly identifiable.

operationalization: Combine dated pollen and fossil occurrences with population genomics and species distribution models to test lowland range continuity during glacial maxima and subsequent isolation on mountains and in the Arctic. Competing preglacial vicariance or independent colonization should predict different dates and routes.

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: dated late-Quaternary pollen and fossil occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: public sequences for arctic-alpine phylogeography

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: current arctic and alpine distributions

obstacles: Pollen often resolves only to genus.
Many species have idiosyncratic glacial refugia.
rationale: Multiple independent public data types record range shifts and population isolation. Species-specific resolution varies, but the historical mechanism is strongly testable for many focal taxa.

operationalization: Infer divergence times and ancestral ranges for temperate sister lineages in North America and Europe, and compare them with Pliocene circumpolar fossils and paleogeography. Support requires northern ancestral ranges and separation dates consistent with southward migration and Atlantic isolation.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Pliocene high-latitude fossil occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data for divergence and ancestral-range analyses

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: modern temperate distributions

obstacles: Divergence-time uncertainty often spans multiple climatic episodes.
Different clades crossed via different routes and times.
rationale: The proposed history yields distinct fossil and phylogeographic predictions for individual clades. Existing coverage is insufficient to make one explanation account for the entire temperate biota.

operationalization: Align independently dated temperature and ice-volume proxies from both hemispheres and across longitudes during the last glacial cycle. Test whether their credible intervals show an overlapping globally cooler interval versus asynchronous regional glaciations.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA World Data Service for Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: public globally distributed paleoclimate proxy records

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: dated marine and terrestrial paleoclimate datasets

obstacles: Regional maxima were not exactly synchronous.
Age-model uncertainty limits fine temporal comparisons.
rationale: Global paleoclimate archives directly and independently measure temperature and ice history. They provide sufficient temporal and spatial coverage to resolve the broad simultaneous-cooling claim.

operationalization: Compare species identity and phylogenetic relatedness among floras of high mountains and temperate lowlands in both hemispheres against distance- and environment-matched null assemblages. Quantify whether related nonidentical pairs substantially outnumber identical pairs.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global plant occurrences across elevation and latitude

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic relatedness among plant taxa

obstacles: Mountain occurrence sampling is uneven.
Species-name synonymy can distort identity counts.
rationale: Modern occurrence, elevation, taxonomy, and phylogeny data map directly to every component of the empirical pattern. Standard null models can distinguish it from simple climatic sorting.

operationalization: Infer direction and counts of cross-equatorial plant migrations through time, then model whether northern land area, inferred source population size, and competitive traits predict southward establishment. Support requires a north-to-south excess mediated by those proposed variables.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: current plant distributions

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeographic inference of migration direction

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Quaternary plant range histories

obstacles: 'Dominating power' has no direct common measure.
Migration direction and extinction can be confounded.
Glacial genomic sampling is sparse in the southern hemisphere.
rationale: Migration asymmetry is testable, but Darwin's population-size and competitive-superiority mechanism requires uncertain proxies. Existing data can resolve parts of the causal chain rather than the full explanation.

operationalization: Count established non-native species introduced from Europe to La Plata and Australia and from the southern hemisphere to Europe, standardized by area, introduction effort, and taxonomic coverage. Compare direction-specific naturalization and displacement rates.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species
candidate_datasets.role: country-level introduced and invasive species inventories

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: native and established occurrence records

obstacles: Historical introduction effort is strongly asymmetric.
Native status and displacement effects are incomplete for some taxa.
rationale: The directional count claim is explicit and global invasion databases contain the needed records. Introduction-pressure adjustment is necessary, but it does not prevent resolving whether the stated asymmetry exists.

operationalization: For southern disjunct plant genera, infer ancestral areas and divergence dates and compare them with Antarctic fossils, paleoclimate, and changing island connections. Support requires Antarctic ancestry during a warm preglacial interval followed by outward lineage splits.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Antarctic and southern-hemisphere plant fossils

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: molecular dating and ancestral-range inference

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: modern disjunct plant distributions

obstacles: Antarctic terrestrial fossil sampling is sparse.
Vicariance can mimic radiating dispersal.
Divergence estimates may not identify former stepping-stone islands.
rationale: The historical scenario has testable fossil and phylogenetic predictions for many genera. Sparse Antarctic evidence and alternative Gondwanan histories prevent full resolution as a general mechanism.

operationalization: Estimate range sizes of freshwater species across major classes and compare their distributions and phylogenetic relatedness among drainage basins worldwide. Test whether broad ranges and global prevalence of related freshwater lineages exceed matched terrestrial expectations.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global freshwater species occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: Freshwater Information Platform
candidate_datasets.role: freshwater biodiversity data and distribution resources

Defining 'enormous' requires class-specific thresholds.
rationale: Large public distribution datasets directly support range and relatedness analyses across many freshwater groups. Coverage is broad enough to test the empirical generalization despite taxonomic gaps.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species distributions, habitats, and native ranges of fishes

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced freshwater-fish occurrences

Taxonomic synonyms and cryptic species can create false sharing or separation.
rationale: The universal continental statement has an obvious falsifier and comprehensive public fish distribution resources. The within-continent component is also a straightforward basin-composition analysis.

operationalization: Link waterbird movement networks with viable seeds or invertebrate eggs recovered from plumage, feet, or digestive tracts and compare resulting connectivity with freshwater species genetic structure. candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: movement tracks of freshwater birds

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: freshwater organism and bird occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public experimental datasets on propagule transport and viability

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: global island and continental species occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF

candidate_datasets.name: Global Island Database

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF

candidate_datasets.role: movement capacity for mobile vertebrate groups

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic framework for repeated growth-form transitions

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: plant growth-form and stature traits

obstacles: Trait coverage is incomplete and some TRY access is conditional.
Woodiness can evolve for drought, longevity, or seasonality rather than competition for height.
Ancestral states and colonization direction can be uncertain.
rationale: Repeated evolution of island woodiness is testable with phylogenies and traits. Existing observational data have weaker power to isolate Darwin's particular selective cause from several modern alternatives.

operationalization: Inventory native amphibians on geologically oceanic islands, distinguish introductions, and relate presence to island origin and sea-crossing distance; combine this with saltwater survival experiments for adults and spawn. Native records on remote true oceanic islands or high salt tolerance would refute the strong claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: amphibian taxonomy, distributions, and natural-history records

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced island amphibian occurrences

obstacles: Some island geological classifications are disputed.
Ancient rafting events can occur despite generally low salt tolerance.
Introduced populations must be removed.
rationale: The distributional statement has clear counterexamples and comprehensive modern databases. The seawater mechanism can also be checked experimentally from published data, making the claim strongly resolvable.

operationalization: Cross-reference native non-volant mammal ranges with island distance and geological origin, excluding human introductions and formerly connected continental islands. A verified native population beyond 300 miles refutes the threshold claim.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: native ranges and status of terrestrial mammals

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: island mammal occurrences

candidate_datasets.name: Global Island Database
candidate_datasets.role: island geography and distance inputs

obstacles: Prehistoric human translocations can masquerade as native populations.
Past sea level altered distances and connections.
rationale: The numerical universal is exceptionally clear and readily falsified using global mammal and island data. Historical introductions require auditing but do not make the analysis impractical.

operationalization: Measure bat occupancy and endemic-species proportions across a global set of islands as functions of isolation, area, and survey completeness, contrasting non-volant mammals. Support requires near-ubiquitous bat presence and elevated endemicity on remote islands.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: bat native ranges and endemic status

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: island bat occurrence records

candidate_datasets.name: Global Island Database
candidate_datasets.role: global island geography

obstacles: Small remote islands are undersurveyed for bats.
'Almost every island' needs an island-size and survey threshold.
rationale: Modern global mammal ranges and island inventories directly test both occupancy and endemicity. Survey completeness can be modeled, leaving high power to confirm or refute the broad pattern.
